props.title: Four Flies on Grey Velvet
props.initialSlug: Drummer stalked by killer with murderous secret

sections.content: Four Flies on Grey Velvet represents Dario Argento at his most experimental, completing his "Animal Trilogy" after The Bird with the Crystal Plumage (1970) and The Cat o' Nine Tails (1971). The film pushes giallo conventions into surreal territory, using groundbreaking high-speed cameras to capture the retinal image of a murder victim - a pseudo-scientific plot device that exemplifies Argento's blend of psychological thriller and technological innovation. Like Deep Red (1975) and Suspiria (1977), the film features elaborate murder sequences choreographed like violent ballet.

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond Italian horror, establishing techniques that would impact later psychological thrillers. The use of unreliable perspective and identity confusion echoes through films like Dressed to Kill (1980) and Basic Instinct (1992). Argento's innovative camera techniques, particularly the reverse-motion photography in the death scenes, influenced horror cinematography for decades, seen in films like Opera (1987) and Trauma (1993). SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Visual Style

Argento collaborated with cinematographer Franco Di Giacomo to create the film's distinctive look, pushing technical boundaries with the pioneering use of the Pentazet lens system. This approach to visual storytelling influenced later directors like Brian De Palma in Phantom of the Paradise (1974) and Blow Out (1981). The film's elaborate sound design, featuring progressive rock elements from Ennio Morricone's score, established a template for giallo soundtracks that would influence horror cinema through the 1970s and beyond.
